items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the ratio of a country’s export prices to its import prices, usually expressed as an index: export price index ÷ import price index × 100”.
items.answer: Terms of trade
items.markingKey: Terms of trade: the ratio of a country’s export prices to its import prices, usually expressed as an index: export price index ÷ import price index × 100. [1]

items.stem: Explain why many LICs experience declining terms of trade.
items.answer: They export primary commodities whose prices are volatile and tend to fall relative to manufactured goods; demand is price-inelastic; many producers compete; synthetic substitutes; tariff escalation discourages processing.

items.stem: Describe the pattern of global trade.
items.answer: Dominated by HICs and East Asia; most trade is between HICs and within regions (EU, East Asia, North America); China is the largest exporter of goods; LDCs account for about 1% of world merchandise exports.

Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Suggest how the country could reduce its vulnerability to changes in the terms of trade.
items.answer: Diversify exports; process commodities at home to add value; develop manufacturing and services; stabilisation funds; Fairtrade and long-term contracts.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Côte d’Ivoire (cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 79, imports 102; 2019: exports 132, imports 112; 2021: exports 112, imports 114; 2023: exports 95, imports 131. (b) Explain what a falling terms of trade means for the country.
items.answer: (a) 2019 (b) It must export more to pay for the same quantity of imports, reducing real income, government revenue and the ability to repay debt.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that dependence on primary commodities is the main reason why some countries gain little from world trade? In your answer you may refer to tariffs, value added and terms of trade.
items.answer: For: Volatile and falling commodity prices, declining terms of trade, little value added (Zambia’s copper, Burundi’s coffee). Against: Tariff escalation, trade rules, lack of infrastructure, conflict, weak institutions and the power of TNCs also limit gains; some commodity exporters gain greatly (Botswana diamonds, Gulf oil). Conclusion: Commodity dependence is a key factor, but governance and the structure of trade rules determine whether countries benefit.

items.stem: Explain the advantages of trade blocs for member countries.
items.answer: Larger markets without tariffs; economies of scale; more foreign investment; increased competition and efficiency; stronger bargaining power in negotiations.

items.stem: Explain why trade blocs may disadvantage non-member countries.
items.answer: Common external tariffs make their exports less competitive (trade diversion); subsidies such as the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy depress world prices.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that fair trade is more effective than free trade in helping LICs benefit from world trade?
items.answer: For: Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and premiums, improving livelihoods for certified farmers (cocoa cooperatives in Ghana such as Kuapa Kokoo). Against: Fairtrade is small-scale; free trade and access to large markets drove growth in East Asia; removal of HIC subsidies and tariff escalation would benefit far more people. Conclusion: Fair trade helps particular producers, but reforms to trade rules and market access have greater potential impact.

items.answer: Earnings depend on the price and demand for ready-made garments; a fall in world prices or demand, or a supply shock, sharply reduces income, revenue and the ability to pay for imports.

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that the pattern of world trade benefits HICs more than LICs.
items.answer: For: HICs and East Asia capture most trade value; LICs export low-value commodities with declining terms of trade; subsidies and tariff escalation. Against: Many LICs and NICs have gained from trade (China, Vietnam, Bangladesh); preferential access schemes; South-South trade is growing; consumers in LICs gain from cheaper imports. Conclusion: The current pattern favours HICs, but countries that diversify into manufacturing and services can benefit greatly.

items.stem: Explain how some LICs and NICs have increased their participation in world trade.
items.answer: Export-oriented manufacturing (Bangladesh garments, Vietnam electronics); joining global value chains; trade agreements and preferential access (EBA, AGOA); investment in ports and SEZs.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why HICs dominate world trade. (b) A student writes: “Landlocked countries face higher trade costs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) They produce high-value manufactured goods and services; have large markets, capital, technology and infrastructure; TNC headquarters; trade rules and institutions shaped by them. (b) Correct. They depend on neighbours’ transport routes and ports.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 23.3 shows the share (%) of export earnings by product for Ethiopia in one year: coffee 74%, oilseeds 5%, cut flowers 18%, gold 2%, other 1%. Total exports were US$60 billion, imports US$79 billion and GDP US$346 billion. Suggest how the country could diversify its exports.
items.answer: Process raw materials domestically; develop other manufacturing and services; invest in infrastructure, education and SEZs; seek trade agreements; promote tourism and horticulture.

items.stem: Felix argues that the pattern of world trade benefits HICs more than LICs. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to trade rules and NICs.
items.answer: For: HICs and East Asia capture most trade value; LICs export low-value commodities with declining terms of trade; subsidies and tariff escalation. Against: Many LICs and NICs have gained from trade (China, Vietnam, Bangladesh); preferential access schemes; South-South trade is growing; consumers in LICs gain from cheaper imports. Conclusion: The current pattern favours HICs, but countries that diversify into manufacturing and services can benefit greatly.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when a large share of a country’s export earnings comes from one or a few primary commodities”.
items.answer: Commodity dependence
items.markingKey: Commodity dependence: when a large share of a country’s export earnings comes from one or a few primary commodities. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Trade in services is growing faster than trade in goods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the pattern of global trade.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Digital, financial and business services trade has expanded rapidly. (b) Dominated by HICs and East Asia; most trade is between HICs and within regions (EU, East Asia, North America); China is the largest exporter of goods; LDCs account for about 1% of world merchandise exports.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [4]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Processing raw materials before export increases value added.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Trade in services is growing faster than trade in goods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Chocolate is worth much more than cocoa beans. (b) Correct. Digital, financial and business services trade has expanded rapidly.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Côte d’Ivoire (cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 78, imports 106; 2019: exports 108, imports 114; 2021: exports 76, imports 108; 2023: exports 96, imports 132. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Suggest why the export price index fluctuated.
items.answer: Commodity prices depend on world demand (Chinese growth), supply from other producers, weather and disease affecting harvests, speculation and exchange rates.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Ethiopia (coffee): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 98, imports 103; 2019: exports 80, imports 111; 2021: exports 138, imports 106; 2023: exports 134, imports 116. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Explain what a falling terms of trade means for the country.
items.answer: It must export more to pay for the same quantity of imports, reducing real income, government revenue and the ability to repay debt.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Ghana (gold and cocoa): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 131, imports 108; 2019: exports 105, imports 109; 2021: exports 107, imports 118; 2023: exports 82, imports 123. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. (a) State the years when the terms of trade were favourable compared with 2015. (b) Explain what a falling terms of trade means for the country.
items.answer: (a) 2017 (b) It must export more to pay for the same quantity of imports, reducing real income, government revenue and the ability to repay debt.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that dependence on primary commodities is the main reason why some countries gain little from world trade?
items.answer: For: Volatile and falling commodity prices, declining terms of trade, little value added (Zambia’s copper, Burundi’s coffee). Against: Tariff escalation, trade rules, lack of infrastructure, conflict, weak institutions and the power of TNCs also limit gains; some commodity exporters gain greatly (Botswana diamonds, Gulf oil). Conclusion: Commodity dependence is a key factor, but governance and the structure of trade rules determine whether countries benefit.

items.stem: Table 23.1 shows export and import price indices (2015 = 100) for Chile (copper): 2015: exports 100, imports 100; 2017: exports 82, imports 103; 2019: exports 83, imports 115; 2021: exports 81, imports 108; 2023: exports 78, imports 118. Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index for each year. (b) State the years when the terms of trade were favourable compared with 2015. items.answer: (a) 2015: 100; 2017: 79.6; 2019: 72.2; 2021: 75; 2023: 66.1 (b) None: the index was at or below 100 in all later years. (c) Commodity prices depend on world demand (Chinese growth), supply from other producers, weather and disease affecting harvests, speculation and exchange rates.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported”.
items.answer: Quota
items.markingKey: Quota: a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the benefits and limitations of Fairtrade. (b) A student writes: “The WTO has removed all barriers to trade.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Benefits: minimum price, premium for schools, clinics and equipment, stable contracts, better conditions. Limitations: small share of world trade, certification costs, benefits may not reach labourers, consumers pay more. (b) Not correct. Many tariffs, subsidies and non-tariff barriers remain.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the benefits and limitations of Fairtrade. (b) A revision website states: “Tariff escalation discourages processing in LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Benefits: minimum price, premium for schools, clinics and equipment, stable contracts, better conditions. Limitations: small share of world trade, certification costs, benefits may not reach labourers, consumers pay more. (b) Correct. Higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials favour exports of unprocessed commodities.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A coffee cooperative member in Peru sells 5 000 lb of coffee. The world market price is US$1.93 per lb. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$1.4 per lb (or the market price if higher), plus a Fairtrade premium of US$0.2 per lb. Calculate the percentage increase in income under Fairtrade.
items.markingKey: (Fairtrade − market) ÷ market × 100 [2]

items.stem: A coffee cooperative member in Peru sells 8 000 lb of coffee. The world market price is US$1.2 per lb. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$1.6 per lb (or the market price if higher), plus a Fairtrade premium of US$0.4 per lb. Explain why coffee farmers often receive a small share of the retail price.
items.answer: Most value is added by roasting, branding and retailing in consumer countries; traders and TNCs take margins; farmers sell unprocessed beans.

items.stem: A coffee cooperative member in Peru sells 8 000 lb of coffee. The world market price is US$1.6 per lb. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$1.8 per lb (or the market price if higher), plus a Fairtrade premium of US$0.4 per lb. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in income under Fairtrade. (b) Explain why coffee farmers often receive a small share of the retail price.
items.answer: (a) +37.5% (b) Most value is added by roasting, branding and retailing in consumer countries; traders and TNCs take margins; farmers sell unprocessed beans.
items.markingKey: (a) (Fairtrade − market) ÷ market × 100 [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: A coffee cooperative member in Peru sells 5 000 lb of coffee. The world market price is US$1.74 per lb. The Fairtrade minimum price is US$1.8 per lb (or the market price if higher), plus a Fairtrade premium of US$0.3 per lb. (a) Explain why the benefits of Fairtrade may be limited. (b) Explain why coffee farmers often receive a small share of the retail price.
items.answer: (a) Cooperatives can sell only part of their crop on Fairtrade terms; certification costs; hired labourers may not benefit; small share of the market; premium shared across members. (b) Most value is added by roasting, branding and retailing in consumer countries; traders and TNCs take margins; farmers sell unprocessed beans.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “export concentration”?
options: The value of exports plus imports as a percentage of GDP.
An EU scheme giving LDCs duty-free, quota-free access for all exports except arms.
The stages of production of a good spread across several countries.
The extent to which a country’s exports depend on a small number of products.
items.answer: The extent to which a country’s exports depend on a small number of products.
items.markingKey: Export concentration: the extent to which a country’s exports depend on a small number of products. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how some LICs and NICs have increased their participation in world trade. (b) A revision website states: “Joining global value chains can help countries industrialise.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Export-oriented manufacturing (Bangladesh garments, Vietnam electronics); joining global value chains; trade agreements and preferential access (EBA, AGOA); investment in ports and SEZs. (b) Correct. Vietnam and Bangladesh grew through assembly and garment exports.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why HICs dominate world trade. (b) Explain the barriers to LIC participation in world trade.
items.answer: (a) They produce high-value manufactured goods and services; have large markets, capital, technology and infrastructure; TNC headquarters; trade rules and institutions shaped by them. (b) Dependence on low-value primary products; poor transport and port infrastructure; landlocked locations; tariffs and non-tariff barriers (standards) in HIC markets; HIC subsidies; lack of finance and skills.
